newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Britain's Major seeks to boost trade in Pakistan.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Major seeks to boost trade in Pakistan.

text.p: LAHORE, Pakistan, Jan 14 (Pakistan) - British Prime Minister John Major flew to the Pakistan city of Lahore on Tuesday on the last leg of a South Asian tour designed to boost trade and political links.
The final day of his week-long tour was packed with visits to British aid schemes, a joint venture project and a seminar given by British businessmen.
Major, who has steered a careful course through the turbulent political scene during his two days in Pakistan, praised the "tremendous untapped potential" of the country.

But underlining the message he has been driving home that Pakistan must not jettison democracy, he added: "Trade and investment will only flourish in the long term against a stable political background."

Major has held talks with both government and opposition leaders including caretaker prime minister Meraj Khalid, Benazir Bhutto, whom Khalid replaced, opposition leader Nawaz Sharif and President Farooq Leghari.

He has stressed that he looks forward to elections due next month to a new National Assembly to replace the one dissolved by Leghari after he dismissed Bhutto as prime minister on disputed charges of corruption and misrule.
But trade has been the official focus of his tour. Officials said the energy company Lasmo Plc announced on Tuesday in Lahore that it had been granted three new oil and gas exploration licences.
The licences are for on- and offshore exploration in the Bela North, Bela South and Kirthar West areas of Pakistan's coast with the Arabian Sea.

The Lahore visit follows a whistle-stop tour on Monday to the top of the Khyber Pass, the route taken by invaders from Darius of Persia to Alexander the Great's generals and warring Afghan tribes, and now the route for most of Europe's heroin.
Major told troops from Pakistan's crack Frontier Corps that Britain would consider making up shortfalls in the equipment they use to try to halt the flow of drugs.
Major was enthusiastically cheered by crowds of brightly clad Pakistani schoolchilden as he arrived in Lahore. The warmth of the reception was typical of the reaction to Major's visit.
He was mobbed in India by businessmen and women, and praised by Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina for his efforts to boost trade.
But the warm glow of his welcome in unlikely to last long on his return to Britain on Tuesday night -- he faces an election just four months away and he is some 20 points behind in the opinion polls.
